title: Enzymes and metabolism
summary: How enzymes act as biological catalysts that control the web of chemical reactions in cells, what affects their activity, and (HL) how metabolic pathways are regulated by inhibition.

keyterms.definition: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being changed or used up by the reaction.
The complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions occurring in living systems, almost all catalysed by enzymes.
Reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones, e.g. condensation reactions forming macromolecules such as glycogen or proteins; require energy.
Reactions that break down larger molecules into smaller ones, e.g. hydrolysis of macromolecules in digestion; often release energy.
The region of a globular enzyme, formed by a small number of amino acids, to which the substrate binds and where catalysis occurs.
Binding of the substrate causes changes in shape of both the substrate and the active site, stressing bonds in the substrate and aiding catalysis.
Each enzyme catalyses one reaction or a group of similar reactions because only substrates with a matching shape and chemical properties fit its active site.
A structural change in a protein, caused by high temperature or extreme pH, that alters the active site so the enzyme can no longer bind substrate; usually permanent.
The energy needed to break bonds in the substrate to start a reaction; enzymes lower it, increasing reaction rate.
The temperature or pH at which an enzyme's rate of reaction is highest.
Inhibition by a molecule that resembles the substrate and binds reversibly to the active site, so it competes with the substrate; overcome by raising substrate concentration.
Inhibition by a molecule binding to an allosteric site, changing the active site shape; raising substrate concentration cannot restore the maximum rate.
A binding site on an enzyme separate from the active site; binding there changes the enzyme's shape and activity.
Regulation of a metabolic pathway in which the end product inhibits an enzyme early in the pathway, usually by binding to its allosteric site.
Irreversible inhibition in which an inhibitor binds covalently to the active site, chemically changing it, e.g. penicillin binding to transpeptidase.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an enzyme?
options: A lipid that supplies energy to a reaction
A globular protein that acts as a biological catalyst
A substrate that is converted into product
A hormone that is used up as it speeds up a reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes are globular proteins that speed up reactions without being used up, so a single enzyme molecule can be used again and again. They do not supply energy; they lower the activation energy.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a catabolic reaction?
options: Formation of glycogen from glucose
Synthesis of a polypeptide at a ribosome
Hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers during digestion
Joining nucleotides to make DNA
questions.explanation: Catabolism breaks large molecules into smaller ones, as in the hydrolysis of macromolecules during digestion. Glycogen formation, protein synthesis and DNA synthesis are anabolic condensation reactions.

questions.statement: The active site of an enzyme is made up of only a relatively small number of the enzyme's amino acids.
questions.explanation: Most of the enzyme's amino acids hold the 3D shape in place; only a few form the active site, which binds the substrate and catalyses the reaction.

questions.text: When a substrate binds, both the substrate and the active site change shape. This model is called ___.
questions.explanation: In the induced-fit model, binding changes the shape of both the active site and the substrate, which stresses bonds in the substrate and makes the reaction easier.

questions.statement: Enzymes speed up reactions by supplying extra energy to the substrate molecules.
questions.explanation: Enzymes do not add energy. They lower the activation energy needed for the reaction, so more substrate molecules can react at a given temperature.

questions.prompt: How does an enzyme affect the energy changes in an exothermic reaction?
options: It increases the activation energy and the energy released
It decreases the energy released by the reaction
It increases the energy of the products
It lowers the activation energy but does not change the overall energy released
questions.explanation: An enzyme provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, but the energy levels of substrate and product are unchanged, so the net energy released stays the same.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: All the enzyme-catalysed reactions in a cell or organism
Building macromolecules from monomers by condensation
Breaking macromolecules into monomers by hydrolysis
Speeds up a reaction without being used up

questions.explanation: Metabolism is the whole network of reactions; it is split into anabolic (building, e.g. protein synthesis) and catabolic (breaking down, e.g. digestion) reactions, which enzymes catalyse.

questions.prompt: Put the events of an enzyme-catalysed reaction in order.
items: Substrate and active site collide due to molecular motion
Substrate binds to the active site
Active site and substrate change shape (induced fit)
Products are released and the active site is free again
questions.explanation: Catalysis depends on a successful collision, then binding and induced fit, which stresses substrate bonds so they are converted to products; the unchanged enzyme then releases the products and can be reused.

questions.text: Substrate–active site collisions happen because of random molecular ___, mostly of the smaller substrate molecules.
questions.explanation: Substrate and enzyme molecules in solution move randomly; the substrate usually moves more because it is smaller. Only collisions with the right orientation lead to binding.

questions.prompt: Why is enzyme specificity essential for controlling metabolism?
options: Each reaction needs its own enzyme, so a cell controls which reactions happen by which enzymes it makes
Specific enzymes can catalyse every reaction in the cell at once
Specificity allows enzymes to work at any temperature
Specific enzymes are not affected by substrate concentration
questions.explanation: Because enzymes are specific, a cell can control its metabolism by controlling which enzymes it synthesises (gene expression) and how active they are.

questions.prompt: Why does the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction increase as temperature rises towards the optimum?
options: The active site becomes larger
More enzyme molecules are synthesised
Molecules have more kinetic energy, so substrate–active site collisions are more frequent
The activation energy of the reaction increases
questions.explanation: Higher temperature increases kinetic energy, so molecules move faster and collide with active sites more often and with more energy, increasing the rate.

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate drops sharply above the optimum temperature.
options: Substrate molecules move too fast to bind
Bonds holding the enzyme's structure break, changing the active site so substrate no longer fits
The enzyme is used up by the reaction
Products accumulate and block the active site
questions.explanation: High temperatures break the bonds (e.g. hydrogen bonds) that maintain the tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape; this is denaturation.

questions.statement: Denaturation of an enzyme by high temperature is usually permanent.
questions.explanation: Once the bonds holding the tertiary structure have broken, the enzyme does not usually regain its shape when cooled, so the activity is permanently lost.

questions.statement: Once substrate concentration is high, doubling it again will double the rate of reaction.
questions.explanation: At high substrate concentration most active sites are occupied at any moment, so the rate levels off (plateaus); extra substrate has little effect.

questions.text: The pH at which an enzyme works fastest is called its ___ pH.
questions.explanation: Each enzyme has an optimum pH; on either side of it the charges on amino acids in the active site change, reducing binding, and extreme pH causes denaturation.

questions.text: A permanent change to the structure of an enzyme so that its active site no longer binds substrate is called ___.
questions.explanation: Denaturation is a structural change caused by heat or extreme pH; the specific shape of the active site is lost, so specificity and activity are lost too.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to the shape of its rate graph.

pairs.right: Gradual rise to optimum, then a steep fall
Peak at optimum, falling on both sides
Rises steeply, then levels off to a plateau

questions.explanation: Temperature curves are asymmetric because denaturation is rapid above the optimum; pH curves peak at the optimum; substrate curves plateau as active sites become saturated.

questions.prompt: In an experiment with catalase, 24 cm³ of oxygen was collected in 2 minutes. What was the mean rate of reaction?
options: 12 cm³ min⁻¹
48 cm³ min⁻¹
0.083 cm³ min⁻¹
24 cm³ min⁻¹
questions.explanation: Rate = amount of product formed ÷ time taken = 24 cm³ ÷ 2 min = 12 cm³ min⁻¹.

questions.prompt: A student investigates the effect of pH on catalase activity. Which should be a controlled variable?
options: pH of the buffer
Volume of oxygen produced
Time taken to collect the gas
Temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.explanation: pH is the independent variable and oxygen produced per unit time is the dependent variable. Temperature also affects enzyme activity, so it must be kept constant.

questions.prompt: Which method measures the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?
options: Recording the final mass of enzyme left
Measuring the amount of product formed, or substrate used, per unit time
Measuring the activation energy with a thermometer
Counting the enzyme molecules at the end
questions.explanation: Rate is change in amount of substrate or product per unit time, e.g. oxygen released by catalase or the disappearance of starch, tested with iodine, when amylase acts.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of an extracellular enzyme-catalysed reaction?
options: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm
The Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix
Digestion of chitin by chitinase secreted by fungi
DNA replication in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Fungi secrete chitinase, which acts outside the cell to break down chitin. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle are intracellular reactions.

questions.statement: Glycolysis is an example of a cyclical metabolic pathway.
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is linear (glucose → pyruvate). The Krebs cycle and the Calvin cycle are cyclical, because the starting compound is regenerated.

questions.prompt: Statins lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting an enzyme in the liver. Which feature shows that this is competitive inhibition?
options: The inhibitor binds permanently to an allosteric site
The inhibitor binds reversibly to the active site, so the inhibition is reduced at high substrate concentration
The inhibitor denatures the enzyme
The inhibitor is the end product of the pathway
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds reversibly to the active site; at high substrate concentration the substrate out-competes it, so the maximum rate can still be reached.

questions.statement: In non-competitive inhibition, increasing the substrate concentration cannot restore the maximum rate of reaction.
questions.explanation: The inhibitor binds to an allosteric site, not the active site, and changes the active site's shape. More substrate cannot displace it, so the maximum rate stays lower.

questions.text: In the pathway that makes isoleucine from threonine, isoleucine inhibits the first enzyme, threonine ___.
questions.explanation: Isoleucine binds to an allosteric site on threonine deaminase (also called threonine dehydratase), slowing the whole pathway when isoleucine is plentiful. This is end-product inhibition.

questions.prompt: Match each inhibitor to its type of inhibition.

pairs.right: Competitive inhibition at the active site
End-product inhibition at an allosteric site

questions.explanation: Statins compete reversibly for the active site; penicillin binds covalently to transpeptidase; isoleucine regulates its own synthesis by allosteric feedback inhibition.

options: It competes reversibly with the substrate of ribosomes
It binds to an allosteric site on DNA polymerase
It denatures all bacterial proteins
It binds irreversibly to the active site of transpeptidase, preventing cross-links in the cell wall
questions.explanation: Penicillin is a mechanism-based inhibitor: it forms a covalent bond in the active site of transpeptidase, so peptidoglycan cross-links are not made and the weakened cell wall bursts.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of end-product inhibition in order.
items: End product accumulates in the cell
End product binds to the allosteric site of the first enzyme
Active site changes shape and binds substrate less readily
Pathway slows and less end product is made
End product concentration falls and the inhibitor detaches
questions.explanation: Feedback inhibition is negative feedback: excess end product switches the pathway off, and as it is used up the inhibition is released, so supply matches demand.

options: Energy transfers in metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient, so some energy is released as heat
Enzymes are heated when they are denatured
Catabolic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings
Heat is needed to raise activation energy
questions.explanation: Metabolic reactions are not fully efficient, so some energy is lost as heat. Mammals and birds use this heat to keep their body temperature constant.

questions.text: The Krebs cycle and the Calvin cycle are examples of ___ metabolic pathways.
questions.explanation: In a cyclical pathway the starting compound is regenerated (oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle, RuBP in the Calvin cycle); linear pathways, like glycolysis, are not.
